claim: A common deleted region (CDR) in both myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) and myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN) affects the long arm of chromosome 20.
source: A common deleted region (CDR) in both myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) and myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN) affects the long arm of chromosome 20 and has been predicted to harbor a tumor suppressor gene.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established background information about the 20q CDR.

claim: The 20q CDR has been predicted to harbor a tumor suppressor gene.
source: A common deleted region (CDR) in both myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) and myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN) affects the long arm of chromosome 20 and has been predicted to harbor a tumor suppressor gene.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction based on prior knowledge about the 20q CDR.

claim: MYBL2 is a gene within the 20q CDR.
source: Here we show that MYBL2, a gene within the 20q CDR, is expressed at sharply reduced levels in CD34+ cells from most MDS cases (65%; n = 26), whether or not they harbor 20q abnormalities.
evidence: The location of MYBL2 within the 20q CDR is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: MYBL2 is expressed at sharply reduced levels in CD34+ cells from 65% of MDS cases (n = 26).
source: Here we show that MYBL2, a gene within the 20q CDR, is expressed at sharply reduced levels in CD34+ cells from most MDS cases (65%; n = 26), whether or not they harbor 20q abnormalities.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by microarray and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Reduced MYBL2 expression in MDS cases occurs whether or not they harbor 20q abnormalities.
source: Here we show that MYBL2, a gene within the 20q CDR, is expressed at sharply reduced levels in CD34+ cells from most MDS cases (65%; n = 26), whether or not they harbor 20q abnormalities.
evidence: This finding is supported by the analysis of both 20q aberrant and normal karyotype MDS cases shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Mybl2 knockdown to 20–30% of normal levels in multipotent hematopoietic progenitors results in clonal dominance of these cells in a murine competitive reconstitution model.
source: In a murine competitive reconstitution model, Mybl2 knockdown by RNAi to 20–30% of normal levels in multipotent hematopoietic progenitors resulted in clonal dominance of these 'sub-haploinsufficient' cells, which was reflected in all blood cell lineages.
evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Clonal dominance from Mybl2 knockdown is reflected in all blood cell lineages.
source: In a murine competitive reconstitution model, Mybl2 knockdown by RNAi to 20–30% of normal levels in multipotent hematopoietic progenitors resulted in clonal dominance of these 'sub-haploinsufficient' cells, which was reflected in all blood cell lineages.
evidence: This is supported by lineage analysis shown in Figure 5D-F demonstrating expansion in lymphocytes and myeloid cells.

claim: By 6 months post-transplantation, mice reconstituted with Mybl2 knockdown cells developed a clonal myeloproliferative/myelodysplastic disorder.
source: By 6 months post-transplantation, the reconstituted mice had developed a clonal myeloproliferative/myelodysplastic disorder originating from the cells with aberrantly reduced Mybl2 expression.
evidence: This is supported by histopathologic analysis shown in Figure 7 and blood count data.

claim: The myeloproliferative/myelodysplastic disorder originates from cells with aberrantly reduced Mybl2 expression.
source: By 6 months post-transplantation, the reconstituted mice had developed a clonal myeloproliferative/myelodysplastic disorder originating from the cells with aberrantly reduced Mybl2 expression.
evidence: This is demonstrated by tracking GFP+ cells with Mybl2 knockdown throughout the experiments.

claim: Downregulation of MYBL2 activity below levels predicted by classical haploinsufficiency underlies clonal expansion of hematopoietic progenitors in a large fraction of human myeloid malignancies.
source: We conclude that downregulation of MYBL2 activity below levels predicted by classical haploinsufficiency underlies the clonal expansion of hematopoietic progenitors in a large fraction of human myeloid malignancies.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the combined clinical and experimental data.

claim: Loss of an interstitial segment of chromosome 20q (20q CDR) is detected in about 4% of myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS).
source: Loss of an interstitial segment of chromosome 20q (20q CDR) is detected in about 4% of myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) (Haase et al., 2007), and this region is variably affected in different types of myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN), including polycythemia vera (10%) and primary myelofibrosis (12%), and less commonly in acute myeloid leukemia (AML; 1%) (Bench et al., 2000).
evidence: This is cited from Haase et al., 2007.

claim: The 20q region is affected in 10% of polycythemia vera cases.
source: Loss of an interstitial segment of chromosome 20q (20q CDR) is detected in about 4% of myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) (Haase et al., 2007), and this region is variably affected in different types of myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN), including polycythemia vera (10%) and primary myelofibrosis (12%), and less commonly in acute myeloid leukemia (AML; 1%) (Bench et al., 2000).
evidence: This is cited from Bench et al., 2000.

claim: The 20q region is affected in 12% of primary myelofibrosis cases.
source: Loss of an interstitial segment of chromosome 20q (20q CDR) is detected in about 4% of myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) (Haase et al., 2007), and this region is variably affected in different types of myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN), including polycythemia vera (10%) and primary myelofibrosis (12%), and less commonly in acute myeloid leukemia (AML; 1%) (Bench et al., 2000).
evidence: This is cited from Bench et al., 2000.

claim: The 20q region is affected in 1% of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cases.
source: Loss of an interstitial segment of chromosome 20q (20q CDR) is detected in about 4% of myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) (Haase et al., 2007), and this region is variably affected in different types of myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN), including polycythemia vera (10%) and primary myelofibrosis (12%), and less commonly in acute myeloid leukemia (AML; 1%) (Bench et al., 2000).
evidence: This is cited from Bench et al., 2000.

claim: Only heterozygous deletions of chromosome 20q have been found in studies of myeloid malignancies, without evidence of homozygous deletion or mutations of a gene within the affected region.
source: Notably, only heterozygous deletions have been found in studies of myeloid malignancies with loss of chromosome 20q, without any evidence of homozygous deletion or mutations of a gene within the affected region (Heinrichs et al., 2009; Huh et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Heinrichs et al., 2009 and Huh et al., 2010.

claim: The findings of only heterozygous deletions implicate a gene within the 20q CDR that is essential for cell viability.
source: These findings implicate a gene within the 20q CDR that is essential for cell viability, but whose tumor suppressor function is strongly dose-dependent and does not follow the classical Knudson model (Knudson, 1971), which predicts biallelic gene inactivation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation of only heterozygous deletions.

claim: The tumor suppressor function of the implicated gene is strongly dose-dependent and does not follow the classical Knudson model.
source: These findings implicate a gene within the 20q CDR that is essential for cell viability, but whose tumor suppressor function is strongly dose-dependent and does not follow the classical Knudson model (Knudson, 1971), which predicts biallelic gene inactivation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of deletions observed and cited knowledge about the Knudson model.

claim: MYBL2 was among the top-scoring genes downregulated in MDS cells with 20q aberrations compared to normal CD34+ controls.
source: We found that MYBL2, which resides near the center of this region (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), was among the top-scoring genes downregulated in MDS cells compared to normal CD34+ controls.
evidence: This is supported by gene expression profiling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: MYBL2 resides near the center of the 20q CDR.
source: We found that MYBL2, which resides near the center of this region (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), was among the top-scoring genes downregulated in MDS cells compared to normal CD34+ controls.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: MYBL2 encodes a highly conserved transcription factor that acts as a major component of the dREAM complex.
source: MYBL2 encodes a highly conserved transcription factor that acts as a major component of the dREAM complex, which controls the G2-to-M phase transition within the cell cycle (Korenjak et al., 2004; Lewis et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from Korenjak et al., 2004 and Lewis et al., 2004.

claim: The dREAM complex controls the G2-to-M phase transition within the cell cycle.
source: MYBL2 encodes a highly conserved transcription factor that acts as a major component of the dREAM complex, which controls the G2-to-M phase transition within the cell cycle (Korenjak et al., 2004; Lewis et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from Korenjak et al., 2004 and Lewis et al., 2004.

claim: The mean expression level of MYBL2 in MDS cases with 20q aberrations was 39% of normal CD34+ cells.
source: The mean expression level of MYBL2 (39%) was less than that of normal CD34+ cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that mechanisms beyond the deletion of one allele might affect the remaining allele.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mechanisms beyond the deletion of one allele might affect the remaining MYBL2 allele.
source: The mean expression level of MYBL2 (39%) was less than that of normal CD34+ cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that mechanisms beyond the deletion of one allele might affect the remaining allele.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that expression is lower than expected from simple haploinsufficiency.

claim: MYBL2 was the top-scoring gene among 108 differentially expressed genes in CD34+ cells from 26 MDS cases compared to normal bone marrow.
source: MYBL2 was the top-scoring gene among 108 differentially expressed genes (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: In 17 (65%) of 26 MDS patients, MYBL2 expression levels in CD34+ cells were reduced to ≤45% of normal CD34+ cells levels (mean 32.8%).
source: Further analysis showed that in 17 (65%) of 26 MDS patients (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), MYBL2 expression levels in CD34+ cells were reduced to ≤45% of normal CD34+ cells levels (mean 32.8%).
evidence: This is supported by microarray data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Microarray data for MYBL2 expression were confirmed by QRT-PCR analysis.
source: These microarray data were confirmed by QRT-PCR analysis of MYBL2 expression levels in 10 MDS cases and eight normal CD34+ bone marrow samples, including four additional normal control CD34+ samples that were not part of the original microarray analysis (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: MYBL2 levels measured by QRT-PCR in MDS samples were highly correlated (r = 0.966) with those determined by microarray analysis.
source: Importantly, MYBL2 levels measured by QRT-PCR in MDS samples were highly correlated (r = 0.966) with those determined by microarray analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This correlation is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: MYBL2 appears to be expressed at reduced levels in nearly two-thirds of MDS cases, including those with a normal karyotype.
source: Hence, MYBL2 appears to be expressed at reduced levels in nearly two-thirds of MDS cases, including those with a normal karyotype, suggesting that it functions as a dose-dependent tumor suppressor gene.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the expression analysis data.

claim: MYBL2 functions as a dose-dependent tumor suppressor gene.
source: Hence, MYBL2 appears to be expressed at reduced levels in nearly two-thirds of MDS cases, including those with a normal karyotype, suggesting that it functions as a dose-dependent tumor suppressor gene.
evidence: This is suggested based on the pattern of expression and the experimental results.

claim: Nearly all differentially expressed genes were downregulated after MYBL2 knockdown (81 of 89 genes).
source: Nearly all differentially expressed genes were downregulated after MYBL2 knockdown (81 of 89 genes; Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) identified mitosis as the key biological process reflected by the MYBL2 gene signature.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) (Subramanian et al., 2005) identified mitosis as the key biological process reflected by the MYBL2 gene signature, specifically the G2-to-M phase transition (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) (Whitfield et al., 2002; Zhu et al., 2004; Shepard et al., 2005).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and cited from multiple sources.

claim: The MYBL2 gene signature specifically reflects the G2-to-M phase transition.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) (Subramanian et al., 2005) identified mitosis as the key biological process reflected by the MYBL2 gene signature, specifically the G2-to-M phase transition (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) (Whitfield et al., 2002; Zhu et al., 2004; Shepard et al., 2005).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and cited from multiple sources.

claim: GSEA revealed robust enrichment of the MYBL2 signature in MDS CD34+ cells.
source: This analysis revealed robust enrichment of the MYBL2 signature in MDS CD34+ cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The expression levels of MYBL2-regulated genes corresponded closely with those of MYBL2 itself.
source: Furthermore, the expression levels of MYBL2-regulated genes corresponded closely with those of MYBL2 itself (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D.

claim: MYBL2 downregulation in CD34+ cells is reflected in the aberrant gene expression profile of a large fraction of MDS cases.
source: Together, these findings indicate that MYBL2 downregulation in CD34+ cells is reflected in the aberrant gene expression profile of a large fraction of MDS cases.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the GSEA and expression correlation analyses.

claim: 10 of 18 normal-karyotype MDS cases (56%) were classified as MYBL2 low using a k-nearest neighbor (KNN) classifier.
source: 10 of these cases (56%) were classified as MYBL2 low, while the remaining eight cases had an MYBL2 signature that was statistically similar to that of normal CD34+ controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: In an independent cohort of 94 normal karyotype MDS cases, 36 cases (38%) had a MYBL2-low signature.
source: To validate our classification algorithm using a separate dataset, we then interrogated the normal karyotype cases (n = 94) reported by Pellagati et al. (Pellagatti et al., 2010), identifying a MYBL2-low signature in 36 cases (38%), most of which (30 cases) were identified at a confidence level of 1.0.
evidence: This is based on analysis of data from Pellagatti et al., 2010.

claim: The 'MYBL2 low' signature is present in CD34+ cells from a substantial fraction of normal-karyotype MDS cases.
source: Thus, we were able to confirm in an independent cohort that the 'MYBL2 low' signature is present in CD34+ cells from a substantial fraction of normal-karyotype MDS cases.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the validation analysis.

claim: Two MDS cases with heterozygous somatic mutations within the MYBL2 coding sequence were identified by resequencing DNA samples from 144 patients.
source: To begin to clarify the mechanism of reduced MYBL2 activity or aberrantly low MYBL2 expression in MDS, we resequenced DNA samples from 144 patients, identifying two cases with heterozygous somatic mutations within the coding sequence that were verified by analysis of patient-specific germline DNA collected from buccal swabs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Both MYBL2 mutations identified were located within the C-terminus.
source: Both mutations, an amino acid substitution and a nonsense mutation, were located within the C-terminus.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the mutations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: SKM1 cells died upon complete knockdown of MYBL2 with an shRNA targeting the 3′UTR.
source: SKM1 cells died upon complete knockdown of MYBL2 with an shRNA targeting the 3′UTR (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The lethality phenotype from MYBL2 knockdown was rescued by re-expression of wild-type MYBL2 cDNA.
source: This phenotype was rescued by re-expression of the wild-type MYBL2 cDNA and the cDNA from patient 28 (Figure 4A), but not by re-expression of the mutated, truncated MYBL2 cDNA of patient 27, which failed to restore the viability of the SKM1 cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The mutated, truncated MYBL2 cDNA from patient 27 failed to restore the viability of SKM1 cells.
source: This phenotype was rescued by re-expression of the wild-type MYBL2 cDNA and the cDNA from patient 28 (Figure 4A), but not by re-expression of the mutated, truncated MYBL2 cDNA of patient 27, which failed to restore the viability of the SKM1 cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A somatically acquired gene-specific inactivating mutation targeting MYBL2 was documented in one case of MDS.
source: Thus, we have documented a somatically acquired gene-specific inactivating mutation that targets MYBL2 in one case of MDS.
evidence: This is based on the functional validation shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Analysis of the MYBL2 CpG island using bone marrow cell DNA from 30 MDS patients failed to detect any methylated cytosines.
source: However, analysis of this site using bone marrow cell DNA from 30 MDS patients failed to detect any methylated cytosines, indicating that DNA methylation is not a frequent mechanism for MYBL2 downregulation in MDS (JP Issa, personal communication, 2012).
evidence: This is based on unpublished data from JP Issa.

claim: DNA methylation is not a frequent mechanism for MYBL2 downregulation in MDS.
source: However, analysis of this site using bone marrow cell DNA from 30 MDS patients failed to detect any methylated cytosines, indicating that DNA methylation is not a frequent mechanism for MYBL2 downregulation in MDS (JP Issa, personal communication, 2012).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the methylation analysis.

claim: A recently published study did not identify methylation affecting the MYBL2 gene in cells from 83 MDS cases.
source: This finding is supported by a recently published study that did not identify methylation affecting the MYBL2 gene in cells from 83 MDS cases (Del Rey et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Del Rey et al., 2012.

claim: mir-29a and mir-30e target MYBL2.
source: We pursued this notion in a subset of patient samples (seven with low MYBL2 expression and two with normal MYBL2 expression, together with three controls) by analyzing the expression levels of mir-29a and mir-30e. Both of these miRNAs target MYBL2 (Han et al., 2010; Martinez et al., 2011), with aberrant expression of mir-29a leading to clonal dominance and acute myeloid leukemia (Han et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Han et al., 2010 and Martinez et al., 2011.

claim: Aberrant expression of mir-29a leads to clonal dominance and acute myeloid leukemia.
source: Both of these miRNAs target MYBL2 (Han et al., 2010; Martinez et al., 2011), with aberrant expression of mir-29a leading to clonal dominance and acute myeloid leukemia (Han et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Han et al., 2010.

claim: Upregulation of either mir-29a or mir-30e was observed in three cases with MYBL2 downregulation, but not in controls or cases with normal MYBL2 expression.
source: Our results show upregulation of either mir-29a or mir-30e in three cases with MYBL2 downregulation, but not in controls or cases with normal MYBL2 expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Overexpression of miRNAs targeting MYBL2 affords an attractive mechanism by which MYBL2 expression levels are lowered in a substantial fraction of MDS cases.
source: Thus, overexpression of miRNAs targeting MYBL2 affords an attractive mechanism by which MYBL2 expression levels are lowered in a substantial fraction of MDS cases.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the miRNA expression analysis.

claim: Five independent shRNA-expressing vectors downregulated Mybl2 expression to levels ranging from 13% (M1) to 33% (M5) of control levels in 32D cells.
source: These vectors downregulated Mybl2 expression to levels that ranged from 13% (M1) to 33% (M5) of those expressed by control shRNA-expressing vectors in 32D cells, a murine myeloid cell line (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Analysis of GFP and RFP levels in peripheral blood at 12 weeks showed a strikingly higher median frequency of GFP+ vs RFP+ cells in mice reconstituted with GFP+/Mybl2-shRNA vs RFP+/control shRNA (30.9% vs 2.6%, p<0.0001).
source: Analysis of GFP and RFP levels in peripheral blood at 12 weeks (Figure 5B) showed a strikingly higher median frequency of GFP+ vs RFP+ cells in the peripheral blood of the mice reconstituted with GFP+/Mybl2-shRNA vs RFP+/control shRNA (30.9% vs 2.6%, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In control mice injected with control/GFP vs control/RFP cells, the median frequencies of both RFP- and GFP-expressing cells were low (1.5% and 3.4%).
source: By contrast, in mice injected with control/GFP vs control/RFP cells, the median frequencies of both RFP- and GFP-expressing cells were low (1.5% and 3.4%; Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: QPCR analysis of mice injected with pools of cells transduced with each of the five shRNAs showed that M3 and M4 were integrated into the DNA of the reconstituted cells that exhibited clonal dominance.
source: These two shRNAs were chosen because QPCR analysis of the mice injected with pools of cells transduced with each of the five shRNAs (Figure 5A) showed that M3 and M4 were integrated into the DNA of the reconstituted cells that exhibited clonal dominance (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Transplanting cells transduced with single Mybl2-specific hairpins (M3 or M4) clearly showed clonal dominance.
source: The results of transplanting cells transduced with single Mybl2-specific hairpins clearly show clonal dominance by cells transduced with either of these vectors (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In a 'color-swap' experiment using the M3 shRNA, bone marrow cells with Mybl2 knockdown became clonally dominant, whether the red or green fluorophore was used.
source: In a 'color-swap' experiment using the M3 shRNA, the bone marrow cells with Mybl2 knockdown became clonally dominant, whether the red or green fluorophore was used (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Downregulation of Mybl2 levels to ∼30% of normal levels using two different Mybl2 shRNAs imparts a strong clonal advantage to hematopoietic progenitor cells.
source: Together, these competitive reconstitution studies firmly establish the surprising finding that downregulation of Mybl2 levels to ∼30% of normal levels using two different Mybl2 shRNAs imparts a strong clonal advantage to hematopoietic progenitor cells, one that becomes reflected in the analysis of circulating white blood cells as early as 12 weeks after transplantation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the competitive reconstitution experiments.

claim: The clonal advantage from Mybl2 knockdown becomes reflected in circulating white blood cells as early as 12 weeks after transplantation.
source: Together, these competitive reconstitution studies firmly establish the surprising finding that downregulation of Mybl2 levels to ∼30% of normal levels using two different Mybl2 shRNAs imparts a strong clonal advantage to hematopoietic progenitor cells, one that becomes reflected in the analysis of circulating white blood cells as early as 12 weeks after transplantation.
evidence: This is based on the peripheral blood analysis at 12 weeks shown in Figures 5B and 6B.

claim: Flow cytometry analysis at 6 to 7 months post-transplantation confirmed expansion of the Mybl2-knockdown cell population compared to control bone marrow cells.
source: The results confirmed expansion of the Mybl2-knockdown cell population compared to control bone marrow cells (Figures 5C and 6D; Figure 8—figure supplement 1C), which surpassed even the percentage of GFP+ cells in the blood (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 5C, 6D, and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Lineage analysis showed that expansion of Mybl2-knockdown cells included lymphocytes as well as myeloid cells.
source: Lineage analysis showed that this expansion included lymphocytes as well as myeloid cells (Figure 5D–F), indicating clonal dominance originating from transduced multilineage long-term repopulating cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D-F.

claim: Clonal dominance originates from transduced multilineage long-term repopulating cells.
source: Lineage analysis showed that this expansion included lymphocytes as well as myeloid cells (Figure 5D–F), indicating clonal dominance originating from transduced multilineage long-term repopulating cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the multilineage expansion shown in Figure 5D-F.

claim: Cells of the myeloid lineage were most prominently affected by Mybl2 knockdown.
source: Cells of the myeloid lineage were most prominently affected, as the frequency of GFP+ cells in the Gr1+/Mac1+ population exceeded 90% in three of five experimental animals.
evidence: This is based on the lineage analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Bone marrow erythropoiesis was reduced by Mybl2 knockdown, as indicated by decreased percentages of Ter119+ cells.
source: Bone marrow erythropoiesis was reduced by Mybl2 knockdown, as indicated by the decreased percentages of Ter119+ cells (Figures 5G–I and 6E; Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 5G-I, 6E, and Figure 8—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Analysis of bone marrow cells expressing the M3 Mybl2-shRNA showed that Mybl2 expression levels were reduced to approximately 20–30% of control levels after long-term reconstitution.
source: As expected, analysis by Western blotting and QRT-PCR of bone marrow cells expressing the M3 Mybl2-shRNA as a single hairpin showed that Mybl2 expression levels were reduced to approximately 20–30% of control levels after long-term reconstitution (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Mybl2 knockdown to 20-30% of control levels does not induce a delay in the G2-to-M-phase transition in bone marrow cells from mice 6–7 months post-transplantation.
source: We did not observe any effect of this level of Mybl2 knockdown on the cell cycle-phase distribution of bone marrow cells from mice 6–7 months post-transplantation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), indicating that this level of decreased Mybl2 expression does not induce a delay in the G2-to-M-phase transition.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Reduced hemoglobin levels indicating anemia were observed in 12 of 13 mice at 6–7 months after transplant.
source: Reduced hemoglobin levels indicating anemia were observed in 12 of the 13 mice (Figure 7A), indicative of the ineffective erythropoiesis in the bone marrow observed by flow cytometry.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Circulating white blood cell and platelet counts were in the normal range in mice at 6-7 months after transplant.
source: Circulating white blood cell and platelet counts were in the normal range.
evidence: This is stated in the text describing the blood count analysis.

claim: Spleen weight was increased in 12 of 13 mice at 6-7 months after transplant, reflecting extramedullary hematopoiesis.
source: Spleen weight was increased in 12 of the 13 mice, reflecting extramedullary hematopoiesis.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The bone marrow in experimental mice was hypercellular and contained more than 95% mature myeloid cells at the expense of erythroid cells (<5%).
source: The bone marrow in experimental mice was hypercellular and contained more than 95% mature myeloid cells at the expense of erythroid cells (<5%), while 2% of the cells had a dysplastic morphology.
evidence: This is based on histopathologic analysis shown in Figure 7F-K.

claim: 2% of bone marrow cells in experimental mice had a dysplastic morphology.
source: The bone marrow in experimental mice was hypercellular and contained more than 95% mature myeloid cells at the expense of erythroid cells (<5%), while 2% of the cells had a dysplastic morphology.
evidence: This is based on histopathologic analysis shown in Figure 7F-K.

claim: The spleens of experimental mice were frequently enlarged, the white pulp was virtually absent, and the whole organ showed evidence of extramedullary hematopoiesis.
source: The spleens were frequently enlarged (Figure 7A), the white pulp was virtually absent, and the whole organ showed evidence of extramedullary hematopoiesis.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A-E.

claim: One mouse developed an erythroid leukemia characterized by a block of differentiation at the CD71-positive stage at 6 months post-transplantation.
source: Notably, one mouse developed an erythroid leukemia characterized by a block of differentiation at the CD71-positive stage at 6 months post-transplantation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The histopathologic findings in mice with Mybl2 knockdown indicate a clonal myeloproliferative disorder with dysplastic features.
source: In summary, the histopathologic findings in these mice indicate a clonal myeloproliferative disorder with dysplastic features.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the histopathologic analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: Within the LSK population of Mybl2-knockdown bone marrow cells, HSCs (CD150+/CD48−) were diminished, MPPs (CD150−/CD48−) were maintained and LRPs (CD150−/CD48+) were increased compared to unlabeled, non-transduced cells.
source: Within the LSK population of GFP+ or RFP+ Mybl2-knockdown bone marrow cells, HSCs (CD150+/CD48−) were diminished, MPPs (CD150−/CD48−) were maintained and LRPs (CD150−/CD48+) were increased compared to unlabeled, non-transduced cells.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The clonal dominance due to low Mybl2 levels is first evident as an increased percentage of cells in the LRP fraction.
source: Thus, the clonal dominance due to low Mybl2 levels is first evident as an increased percentage of cells in the LRP fraction. (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Analysis of blood samples from secondary recipients at 10 weeks revealed a marked clonal advantage for GFP+/Mybl2-RNAi cells transplanted from each of the four mice with primary disease, regardless of whether the cell source was spleen or bone marrow.
source: Analysis of blood samples collected from secondary recipients at 10 weeks revealed a marked clonal advantage for GFP+/Mybl2-RNAi cells transplanted from each of the four mice with primary disease, regardless of whether the cell source was spleen or bone marrow (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8A.

claim: There was evidence of anemia (low RBC and low Hb levels) and thrombocytopenia in 9 of 13 secondary recipient animals.
source: In addition, there was evidence of anemia (low RBC and low Hb levels) and thrombocytopenia in 9 of 13 animals (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The bone marrow of secondary recipients was dominated by GFP+/Mybl2-RNAi cells and showed decreased levels of erythropoiesis as well as histologic evidence of a myeloproliferative disorder with dysplasia.
source: The bone marrow of secondary recipients was also dominated by GFP+/Mybl2-RNAi cells (Figure 8C) and showed decreased levels of erythropoiesis (Figure 8D) as well as histologic evidence of a myeloproliferative disorder with dysplasia.
evidence: This is shown in Figures 8C and 8D.

claim: The phenotypic consequences of Mybl2 knockdown were much more pronounced in secondary compared to primary recipients.
source: Overall, the phenotypic consequences of Mybl2 knockdown were much more pronounced in secondary compared to primary recipients.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the data from primary and secondary transplants.

claim: Secondary transplantation assays show that either spleen or bone marrow cells from mice with myeloid neoplasia due to shRNA-mediated reduced Mybl2 expression can efficiently transmit the blood disorder to secondary recipients.
source: Thus, our secondary transplantation assays show that either spleen or bone marrow cells from mice with myeloid neoplasia due to shRNA-mediated reduced Mybl2 expression can efficiently transmit the blood disorder to secondary recipients.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the secondary transplantation experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: The disorder caused by reduced Mybl2 expression is cell autonomous.
source: This indicates that the disorder is cell autonomous and that hematopoietic progenitor cells with reduced Mybl2 expression can self-renew after transplantation and undergo sustained expansion leading to clonal dominance.
evidence: This is inferred from the successful transmission of the disorder through secondary transplantation.

claim: Hematopoietic progenitor cells with reduced Mybl2 expression can self-renew after transplantation and undergo sustained expansion leading to clonal dominance.
source: This indicates that the disorder is cell autonomous and that hematopoietic progenitor cells with reduced Mybl2 expression can self-renew after transplantation and undergo sustained expansion leading to clonal dominance.
evidence: This is inferred from the successful transmission of the disorder through secondary transplantation.

claim: None of the molecular lesions convincingly linked to MDS pathogenesis affect more than a fourth of cases overall, with a prevalence of 1–15% being much more common.
source: Yet, the disease remains very heterogeneous and none of the molecular lesions that have been convincingly linked to MDS pathogenesis affect more than a fourth of cases overall, with a prevalence of 1–15% being much more common (Bejar et al., 2011; Shih et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Bejar et al., 2011 and Shih et al., 2012.

claim: MYBL2 has been implicated as a gene that is typically overexpressed in several types of cancer.
source: This result is somewhat surprising given that MYBL2 has been implicated as a gene that is typically overexpressed (rather than downregulated) in several types of cancer and whose elevated expression correlates with a poor prognosis in human breast cancer and other malignancies (Amatschek et al., 2004; Paik et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from Amatschek et al., 2004 and Paik et al., 2004.

claim: Elevated MYBL2 expression correlates with a poor prognosis in human breast cancer and other malignancies.
source: This result is somewhat surprising given that MYBL2 has been implicated as a gene that is typically overexpressed (rather than downregulated) in several types of cancer and whose elevated expression correlates with a poor prognosis in human breast cancer and other malignancies (Amatschek et al., 2004; Paik et al., 2004).
evidence: This is cited from Amatschek et al., 2004 and Paik et al., 2004.

claim: No direct evidence demonstrating oncogenic activity by overexpressed MYBL2 has been reported to date.
source: However, no direct evidence demonstrating oncogenic activity by overexpressed MYBL2 has been reported to date.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature.

claim: The proliferative fraction of cells in myeloid neoplasia is generally quite low.
source: By contrast, the proliferative fraction of cells in myeloid neoplasia is generally quite low.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about myeloid neoplasia.

claim: Abnormally low levels of MYBL2 expression have the unique property of imparting a clonal advantage to multipotent hematopoietic progenitors.
source: Our findings demonstrate the surprising finding that abnormally low levels of MYBL2 expression have the unique property of imparting a clonal advantage to multipotent hematopoietic progenitors, leading rapidly to the clonal dominance of such cells within the myeloid, and B- and T-lymphocyte cell lineages.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The affected multipotent hematopoietic cells have both self-renewal and long-term repopulating ability.
source: The persistence of clonal dominance in recipient mice for more than 6 months after bone marrow cell transplantation, and in recipients of secondary transplants, indicates that the affected multipotent hematopoietic cells have both self-renewal and long-term repopulating ability (Morrison and Weissman, 1994).
evidence: This is inferred from the persistence of clonal dominance and cited from Morrison and Weissman, 1994.

claim: MYBL2 is a key tumor suppressor gene of the 20q CDR affected in human MDS and MPD.
source: Hence, our finding establishes MYBL2 as a key tumor suppressor gene of the 20q CDR affected in human MDS and MPD.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined clinical and experimental findings.

claim: Haploinsufficiency for other genes within the 20q CDR may cooperate with aberrantly low expression of MYBL2 to move cells toward malignant transformation.
source: However, we cannot exclude the possibility that haploinsufficiency for other genes within the 20q CDR cooperates with aberrantly low expression of MYBL2 to move the cells toward malignant transformation, as has been shown for the CDR associated with the 5q-syndrome, where haploinsufficiency of the gene RPS14 as well as loss of expression of an miRNA (Ebert et al., 2008; Barlow et al., 2010; Starczynowski et al., 2010) are critical steps in MDS pathogenesis.
evidence: This is speculation based on analogy to the 5q-syndrome and cited from multiple sources.

claim: Haploinsufficiency of RPS14 and loss of expression of an miRNA are critical steps in MDS pathogenesis associated with the 5q-syndrome.
source: However, we cannot exclude the possibility that haploinsufficiency for other genes within the 20q CDR cooperates with aberrantly low expression of MYBL2 to move the cells toward malignant transformation, as has been shown for the CDR associated with the 5q-syndrome, where haploinsufficiency of the gene RPS14 as well as loss of expression of an miRNA (Ebert et al., 2008; Barlow et al., 2010; Starczynowski et al., 2010) are critical steps in MDS pathogenesis.
evidence: This is cited from Ebert et al., 2008; Barlow et al., 2010; Starczynowski et al., 2010.

claim: Interstitial deletion of chromosome 20q is not the only mechanism by which MYBL2 activity can be reduced in MDS.
source: Most intriguing is our finding of decreased MYBL2 expression in MDS cases with a normal karyotype, which suggests that interstitial deletion of chromosome 20q is not the only mechanism by which MYBL2 activity can be reduced in MDS.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding of low MYBL2 expression in normal karyotype cases.

claim: Overexpression of mir-29a in murine bone marrow cells leads to acute myeloid leukemia.
source: In addition, others have shown that overexpression of mir-29a in murine bone marrow cells leads to acute myeloid leukemia (Han et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from Han et al., 2010.

claim: mir-29a may be oncogenic, at least in part, because it targets Mybl2 transcripts.
source: Combined with our results, this observation suggests that mir-29a may be oncogenic, at least in part, because it targets Mybl2 transcripts.
evidence: This is speculation based on combining the cited finding with the current results.

claim: The MYBL2 transcription factor gene is targeted by diverse molecular events in MDS, including deletion within the 20q chromosomal region, heterozygous loss-of-function mutations, and repression of gene expression by dysregulated miRNAs.
source: Thus, our results indicate that the MYBL2 transcription factor gene is targeted by diverse molecular events in MDS, including not only deletion within the 20q chromosomal region, but also heterozygous loss-of-function mutations and the repression of gene expression by dysregulated miRNAs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the multiple mechanisms identified in the study.

claim: Clarke et al. described an association between MYBL2 expression levels and the occurrence of hematologic disorders, including MDS, in aged Mybl2 haploinsufficient mice.
source: Clarke et al. (Clarke et al., 2012) have also described an association between MYBL2 expression levels and the occurrence of hematologic disorders, including MDS, in aged Mybl2 haploinsufficient mice.
evidence: This is cited from Clarke et al., 2012.

claim: Haploinsufficiency for the Mybl2 gene increases susceptibility to age-related myeloid neoplasia.
source: These authors were able to show that haploinsufficiency for the Mybl2 gene increases susceptibility to age-related myeloid neoplasia.
evidence: This is cited from Clarke et al., 2012.

claim: More pronounced gene dosage reduction of Mybl2 might be even more advantageous for clonal dominance than simple haploinsufficiency.
source: Our data indicate that more pronounced gene dosage reduction of Mybl2 might be even more advantageous for clonal dominance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing optimal effects at 20-30% expression.

claim: The oncogenic effects of reduced MYBL2 dosage are more pronounced as the dosage level falls to near 30% of normal, in keeping with the continuum model of tumor suppression.
source: Although our findings do not rule out a causal role for straight-forward haploinsufficiency in myeloid malignancies, they strongly suggest that the oncogenic effects of reduced MYBL2 dosage are more pronounced as the dosage level falls to near 30% of normal, in keeping with the continuum model of tumor suppression (Berger et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and cited from Berger et al., 2011.

claim: The reductions of MYBL2 gene dosage in CD34+ cells from MDS clinical samples were predominately in the range of 20–30% of normal levels.
source: We would also stress that in the range of MYBL2 dosage reductions in this study were modeled based on those found in CD34+ cells from MDS clinical samples, in which the reductions of MYBL2 gene dosage were predominately in the range of 20–30% of normal levels, and thus were considerably lower than the 50% predicted by classical haploinsufficiency.
evidence: This is stated based on the clinical sample analysis.

claim: Expression levels of MYBL2 lower than 20% appear incompatible with cell growth.
source: Importantly, expression levels lower than 20% appear incompatible with cell growth (Figure 4B), consistent with the known function of MYBL2 as a key regulator of G2-to-M transition and the fact that biallelic inactivation of this gene causes early embryonic lethality in the mouse due to a block in inner cell mass formation during embryonic development (Tanaka et al., 1999).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B and cited from Tanaka et al., 1999.

claim: Biallelic inactivation of MYBL2 causes early embryonic lethality in the mouse due to a block in inner cell mass formation during embryonic development.
source: Importantly, expression levels lower than 20% appear incompatible with cell growth (Figure 4B), consistent with the known function of MYBL2 as a key regulator of G2-to-M transition and the fact that biallelic inactivation of this gene causes early embryonic lethality in the mouse due to a block in inner cell mass formation during embryonic development (Tanaka et al., 1999).
evidence: This is cited from Tanaka et al., 1999.

claim: Earlier studies have implicated progressive inactivation of CTNNA1 and graded reduction of PU.1 expression in the molecular pathogenesis of myeloid malignancies.
source: Our results implicating a transforming role for sub-haploinsufficient levels of MYBL2 build upon earlier studies implicating progressive inactivation of CTNNA1 and the graded reduction of PU.1 expression in the molecular pathogenesis of myeloid malignancies (Rosenbauer et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from Rosenbauer et al., 2004 and Liu et al., 2007.
